19397,ca.proc.d.1901-05-09.4.4.1,1901-05-09,6e709d61-48a8-4abc-ac0f-a0e806704351,ca.m.8006,Mr. L. P. DEMERS (St. John and Iberville).,,SUPPLY-ROYAL MINT.,ALIENS' ESTATES-CONVENTION BETWEEN GREAT BRITAIN AND THE UNITED STATES.,,(Translation.) Mr. Speaker, before the House goes into Committee of Supply, I wish to call the attention of the government to the fact that a convention was passed between Great Britain and the United States, which was signed on the 2nd of March, 1899, and ratified on the 28th of July, 1900. According to that convention the United States are ready to give up in favour of Great Britain and of her colonies the right of aiibaine and the right of detraction, both of which the different states, in the middle ages, had arrogated, as we all know. The right of aubaine was the right for the state to seize upon the pro-Mr. PRIOR.
perty of a deceased foreigner. According to common law in England, aliens could own real estate and they can do so even nowadays, but they are not allowed to bequeath it.

Some of the states of the union have yet special provisions affecting the rights of foreigners to acquire and transfer property, but in most of the states, the law is that foreigners are treated as natives in this respect. As I have just said, aliens, in the middle ages, were not at liberty to dispose of their property, they could acquire or own property, but they were forbidden to. dispose of it ; in the event of their death, their wealth devolved to the public treasury.

In France, when the heirs of a deceased person were aliens the public treasury used to get a large portion of that person's property, by virtue of a right known as the right of detraction, and which still exists in some states. That capital is liable to very heavy taxes, whenever it happens to fall into the hands of foreigners.

The United States are ready to give up those rights, which seem to have been given up by all other nations, especially since the French revolution, in 1790, has done away with the right of aiibaine and the right of detraction, without exacting any reciprocity. However, the reciprocity system was again taken up and adopted by the Code Napoleon; but it was finally abolished by the law of the 4th July, 1819, which has placed all aliens in France on an even standing by the fact that it lias abolished the right of aiibaine absolutely and without any view of reciprocity whatsoever.

There is positively no objection to the convention between Great Britain and the United States inuring to the benefit of Canada, for all the provinces have adopted this same view. We have given up that exorbitant right which existed by virtue of common law in England and in all European countries as well throughout the middle ages.

No later than 1894 did United Canada give up that right when she adopted for the provinces of Quebec and Ontario a law according to which foreigners were allowed to acquire and transfer property on the same basis and to the same extent as were all the subjects of-the state. A law of a similar nature was enacted in all the other provinces of Confederation. For instance, in Nova Scotia, aliens were, as early as 1854, permitted to own property and to dispose of it as they would feel proper, and the law which authorises them so to do, can be found in the Revised Statutes of Nova Scotia, 1900, chap. 136. Prince Edward Island followed in 1859. True, it is that an alien cannot own more than two hundred acres of land in that province, but this restriction is undoubtedly due to the fact that the island is rather small. The law with respect to Prince Edward Island is 22 Vic., chap. 4.

Then we have had Manitoba, in 1891; the law which is contained in chap. 3a of the Revised Statutes was adopted there and it has been binding ever since February 28th, 1874. British Columbia voted a law of that kind in 1888, and it has been incorporated in chap. 6 of the Revised Statutes of 1897. New Brunswick also adopted, in 1891, a law which is known as 54 Victoria, chap. 13. Then, legal dispositions of a similar nature are in existence in every province of the Dominion, according to which foreigners and natives are equally unimpeded as far as acquisition of or parting with property is concerned.

As I have said at the beginning of these few remarks, the United States offer to give the citizens of Great Britain and those of her colonies as well, and on the basis of reciprocity, the right to own and to freely dispose of property, just as the American citizens themselves may do, within the limits of the Union. It is enacted by section 4 of that treaty, that it shall not inure to the benefit of any of the English colonies until the Secretary of State has been notified in the name of such colony by Great Britain's representative at Washington within a year from the date on which the treaty or convention has been ratified. My object in raising this question is to ask the government to take such steps as may be necessary to make the American Secretary of State aware, through England's representative, and before the 28th of July, 1901, that the Dominion of Canada is anxious to partake of the advantages of that treaty.

,Liberal,,Louis Philippe Demers,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=6e709d61-48a8-4abc-ac0f-a0e806704351&Language=E&Section=ALL
19398,ca.proc.d.1901-05-09.4.4.2,1901-05-09,intervention,,,,SUPPLY-ROYAL MINT.,ALIENS' ESTATES-CONVENTION BETWEEN GREAT BRITAIN AND THE UNITED STATES.,,In September, 1900, a circular letter was received by the Governor General relating to the convention between the United Kingdom and the United States in regard to real and personal property, and asking His Excellency to refer the letter to his advisers to find out if there was any objection on the part of Canada to becoming a party to the convention. Immediately after that letter was received, it was referred to the different provinces, all of whom declared that they were willing to participate in the convention, or rather to become parties to it, with the exception of New Brunswick. The province of New Brunswick objected on the ground that with respect to succession duties they had a law in that province under which the estates of foreigners were obliged to pay a tax double that which was paid by those who lived in the province. We have had some correspondence with New Brunswick for the purpose of endeavouring to get them to come in with what appears to be the general desire of Canada in this matter, but nothing has been done up to the present time. I may say, however, that it is within the power of the Dominion of Canada to pjroceed in this matter under

section 132 of the British North America Act, without the assent of New Brunswick, if it should be withheld. I believe that there is a general desire that it should come into this convention. It is possible that proceeding under the section referred to we may enter the convention, but I may say that I have hopes that New Brunswick will not persist in the objection. My hon. friend (Mr. Demers) is very anxious that the government should participate in this convention, and it is largely due to his persistent efforts that so much progress has been made up to the present.

,,,The SOLICITOR GENERAL (Hon. Chas. Fitzpatrick).,

TAYLOR (South Leeds).,Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942),SUPPLY-ROYAL MINT.,RENTING OF PRIVATE BUILDINGS BY THE GOVERNMENT.,,Mr. Speaker, before you leave the Chair, I will have a few words to say in reference to the extravagant manner in which this government is managing the affairs of the country. I remember, every one in this House remembers, and the people of Canada remember, that previous to 1S96 when the Prime Minister travelled from the Atlantic to the Pacific, he promised the people that if he were returned to power he would surround himself with a cabinet of business men, and would manage the affairs of the country on business principles. He promised that he would run the business of the country for three or four million dollars less than the then expenditures, and the Hon. David Mills pledged his word that the Liberals would conduct the public business for $5,000,000 less than the Conservatives, who at that time were expending $38,000,000 a year. The Prime Minister promised to practice economy in every shape and form. I ask the right hon. gentleman, and I ask this House, if these promises have been implemented ? Did he surround himself with a cabinet of business men ? Where are the business men in that cabinet ? Just stand them up one after the other and call the roll.

19416,ca.proc.d.1901-05-09.4.5.17,1901-05-09,47b47c19-8fe1-4407-b84f-9029f6aec230,ca.m.2900,Air. TAYLOR.,Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942),SUPPLY-ROYAL MINT.,RENTING OF PRIVATE BUILDINGS BY THE GOVERNMENT.,,Now we come to the last business man in the Cabinet, the hon. Alinister of Customs (Hon. Mr. Paterson), a manufacturer. He knew enough about business when he was making changes in the tariff not to interfere with the duties on biscuits and confectionery. Then we come to two other business men, the gentlemen without portfolio, who have no departments to administer. One of these gentlemen, the hon. member for Quebec AArest (Hon. Air. Dobell), knows something about business ; but this government, instead of allowing him to bring his business ability into play, kept him trotting across the ocean to look after bottle-necked ships. Then we come to the other gentleman without portfolio, my hon. friend from North Oxford (Hon. Air. Sutherland),

who knows more about business than all the rest of the cabinet put together, but who has no department to administer. We have this cabinet of sixteen or seventeen members, nearly all lawyers, although the Prime Minister promised the people of this country that he would surround himself with able and competent business men, who would run this country in a practical business manner.

Now, let me point to one fact. This government knew in 1896, when they took office, that in 1901 the census would have to be taken. What did they do to provide rooms for the accommodation of the census staff ? Did they take a business view of the matter ? Would any business concern in this country, if they wanted to enlarge their premises so as to employ a few more hands, rent a place on the main business street of the city at five or six times the rent at which they could get premises equally good in some other part of the city ; or would they put up a building of their own ? When the late government took the census in 1891, Mr. Johnson, the statistician, supervised the work, and I will guarantee that the work was as well done then as it will be now ; and his whole staff were accommodated in the Langevin block. Hon. gentlemen opposite, when they sat on this side of the House, declared that the buildings were crowded with civil servants, who were tumbling over each other, and that if they came in they would dismiss a few of them. What have they done ? They have employed Mr. Blue as commissioner at a salary of $4,000, and Mr. C6te as assistant commissioner at $3,000, and they have given Mr. St. Denis an increase of salary of $600, making nearly $8,000 in additional salaries to supervise the work ; whereas Mr. George Johnson, who did it before, could have done it again without any extra help, and have saved that $8,000 to the country. Besides, in 1891 one commissioner was employed for each county; but now in most of the counties, particularly those in which a few French are living, there are two commissioners employed. The law says that there shall be one for every electoral district ; but in almost every electoral district in Ontario and Quebec, where there are French and English, there are two commissioners appointed. Now, this government knew in 1896 that the census would have to be taken in 1901, and what provision did they make for getting room for the work in case there should not be room in our own buildings ? They waited until the elections of 1900 were at hand, and then, without their calling by advertisement for premises to rent, without their making any provision at all, a gentleman, who is the proprietor of a building on Sparks street, which has been lying practically idle for the last two or three years, goes to the Minister of Public Works and has a private conversation with him. tleman writes a letter to the acting minister, the Postmaster General (Mon. SOPER.,,Speaking only from memory on the spur of the moment, they are Liverpool, Glasgow, j Manchester, Cardiff, Bristol, London, Newcastle and Dundee. These scheduling of our cattle has been a grievance which we Canadians have protested against again and again. When 1 was last in England I interviewed the Minister of Agriculture there, and took very strong ground, but without the slightest avail. I may inform the hon. gentleman and the committee that at the present time a very strongly worded mem-oradum is on its way to Great Britain on that subject, and I hope to follow that up when I go to England, as I hope to do within a few weeks, with the most strenuous representations against the injustice and unfairness of scheduling our cattle, which not only affects our trade with Great Britain, but which constitutes an aspersion, I might almost say a libel, against the health of our Canadian cattle. We say, and I think I can prove, that there has never been iu the Dominion of Canada a case of contagious pleuro-pneumonia. The excuse given for the scheduling of our cattle in England was the supposed finding in 1802 of three cases of what the English veter-iuaries called pleuro-pneumonia; but our veterinaries in this country took the opportunity of examining the lungs of those animals, and they were strongly of opinion, and asserted it strongly, that these cases were simply eases of what as called transit pleuropneumonia, which is not contagious. Cases of the same kind had occurred before and the cattle had been accepted, the Imperial authorities acknowledging that they were not contagious pleuro-pneumonia, but only transit pleuro-pneumonia; and the cases on which the schedule was founded were identical with those. So strongly am I convinced that they were not cases of contagious pleuro-pneumonia that I would not hesitate to argue the case out. Contagious pleuro-pneumonia is an exceedingly contagious disease. The animals affected by it have to be strictly quarantined, as the disease is sure to spread with great rapidity and virulence. The districts of Canada from which the animals in question came in 1S92 were thoroughly searched; yet not a single case of contagious pleuro-pneumonia was found in them. Those districts were watched afterwards with the greatest assiduity; yet no case of contagious pleuropneumonia has ever been found in the country. It is beyond the power of belief that contagious pleuro-pneumonia could have occurred in that part of the country without the disease spreading and other cases being fouiid; but from that day to this not a single case has been found in Canada, and since that time we have sent to England nearly 800.000 head of cattle, all of which have been inspected by the authorities in England at the point of debarkation. Not one case of contagious pleuro-pneumonia Mr. HUGHES (Victoria).

J was found in any one of the 800,000 Canadian cattle slaughtered there. If pleuropneumonia existed in this country, it is incredible that some case would not have been discovered, either by our own veterinarians, who are always on the look-out for it, or amongst those 800,000 cattle sent to England and slaughtered during those eight years, under the inspection of the Dejiartmeut of Agriculture there. Under the circumstances, the Imperial authorities have not a leg to stand on. They may continue scheduling our cattle, but I have already protested by despatch, and propose in person to present the case to the Canadian farmers and stock dealers against this aspersion cast upon the health of our cattle in Canada- an aspersion which affects us in the trade there and elsewhere, because it is an announcement to the world that the Imperial authorities consider Canada a dangerous country from which to import cattle. It is unfair and improper for the government at the centre of the empire to cast such an aspersion upon an important part of the empire. Every argument will be placed before the authorities with all the strength I am capable of, and I trust will have some effect, because while the Imperial authorities are naturally anxious to safeguard the interests of the inhabitants of the British Isle, they still are imbued by a sense of justice, and a desire for Imperial unity, which may at this time be effective.

SOPER.,,I am much pleased to hear that the hon. the Minister of Agriculture is still pegging away along the line he started on a couple of years ago, when I first brought this matter before liis notice. At present Canadian cattle entering British markets are somewhat handicapped as compared with the cattle of other nations, which may be classed as Britain's enemies -for instance, Germany and Russia. The cattle from Russia enter Britain to-day on better terms than Canadian cattle, owing to the shortness of haulage and cheapness of freight rates. In other words, Canada, an ally of Great Britain, a country that does not cost Great Britain a farthing for defence or offence, is handicapped in the British market by Russia.

If our cattle can enter Wales, England and Scotland, why should they not enter Ireland? We have a line of steamers which trade largely in winter between the maritime provinces, and in summer Quebec and Montreal ports and the old land, and then on to the Baltic and Norway ports, bringing the produce of this country to the markets of the old world. Could that steamship company carry cattle on the decks of its vessels, the freights would be considerably reduced, because a very large competing line would be thus brought into the market for the cattle trade. At
steamers only take part cargoes, so to speak, and the freight rates must, therefore, be higher than they would be if they

could take on deck-loads of cattle. I trust tliat tlie bon. minister will endeavour, now that the British public shows a disposition to move, to place the demands of the Canadian people in this matter before the British authorities. There is no reason in the world why Canadian cattle should not be shipped direct to Belfast and Dublin, and there slaughtered, just as they are now sent to Liverpool and other English ports. There is no reason why cattle should not be brought to Belfast and Dublin and there 'slaughtered, and the carcasses sent to Liverpool and other English and Scotch cities for distribution. There will be no more danger of disease in Ireland than there is in England. Cattle are brought to and fro between England and Ireland, so that if there should be any disease in England, it is certain to be brought to Ireland, and vice versa, and there is no satisfactory reason why the vessels I have referred to should not have the privilege of carrying deckloads of Canadian cattle. lam satisfied that if these enormous steamers have become engaged in the carrying trade of cattle, the freight rates would have been reduced materially and the Canadian farmers have profited.

I have often thought that the present government lost the golden opportunity to secure this great privilege, which they had in 1897, when they proffered to the people of Great Britain a preference in the market of Canada. The government then should certainly have insisted on our obtaining in return a preference for some of the products of Canada in the markets of Great Britain. But, they failed to take advantage of that opportunity, and they failed, no doubt, because of their extreme free trade principles. But, since we have no contagious diseases among our cattle, it is the duty of this government, who are watching or should be watching in the interests of the farmers, to make an effort to have that embargo removed, so that our cattle may be taken freely to any part of Great Britain. We know that cattle taken across the Atlantic will often shrink in weight; and consequently, if they have to be slaughtered at the port of entry, it is a decided disadvantage to the shippers. If the graziers were allowed to purchase the cattle and fatten them on their farms, these cattle would bring nearly as good prices as the fat cattle. The government are not to blame for what the British government did, but they will be to blame if they do not make an effort to have that embargo removed. I think also that the government will be to blame if they do not make an attempt to establish abattoirs where our cattle can be slaughtered, the dead meat being shipped to England, making such an industry as they have in Chicago. I believe that capital can be secured to establish that industry. If it were established, we should have the offal and by-products which could be made the basis of other industries. The hides could be manufactured into leather on this side, and other manufactures could be carried on. Besides, the loss through the shipping of the live animals could be avoided. I have taken cattle across the Atlantic, and I know well the difficulties involved in the attempt to land the cattle in Liverpool, London, or Glasgow, in as good condition as when leaving here. I think it is the duty of the government to try to encourage capital to go into the dead meat trade. I do not like to hear it said that it is on account of the preferential tariff that we do not carry on a larger cattle business with Great Britain. As I said the other night, I wish we had the duty still further lowered and a still greater preference given. Great Britain gives us a free market for everything we wish to send,

except tobacco and whisky-and cattle when they have tuberculosis. And we give her a preference of 33A per cent. Let us look at this thing fairly. Instead of saying that Great Britain is trying to take advantage of us, we should acknowledge that it is rather Canada that is trying to take advantage of Great Britain. As we are part and parcel of this great empire, I think we ought to treat Great Britain fairly. I hope the Minister of Agriculture will discharge his duty faithfully, and will secure such changes that the farmers of this country will be able to send their cattle to any part of Great Britain, if those cattle are free from disease.

SOPER.,,The argument of my hon. friend (Mr. Wallace), that the small trade done at Sorel does not justify this expenditure, is no argument whatever in this case. Sorel has great natural advantages, and if its trade it not larger than it is at present it is simply because there is no such accommodation as is contemplated under this vote. Not later than five years ago, I do not think there was a single dollar's worth of imports or exports at Parry Sound. There is a large trade there now, which has grown up in consequence of the accom-

modation which has been given to that locality. And so it is with Sorel, which is to-day a growing and thriving town of about 8,000 souls, at the junction of the St. Lawrence and Richelieu rivers. The Richelieu river is one of the most important of the many important rivers which we have in the province of Quebec. It is the outlet of Lake Champlain, and it waters one of the finest valleys in the world without any exception, even in the province of Ontario. It waters five or six of the best counties of the Dominion-VerchSres, Rouville, Richelieu, St. Hyacinthe, Iberville, St. John, Bagot and Missisquoi. Many years ago there was a very large and important trade at Sorel, because it was the outlet for that section of the country. That was previous to the era of railway transportation. Since the railways have been established, the trade of Sorel has gone down, and has been transferred to Montreal, which is allied with that section of country by railways. Afler the railways were built, the counties which I have named had no means of export except by railway to Montreal. Some of the lines of railway have been consolidated. The South Eastern, the United Counties, and the Rutland system are all concentrated under one management. It is manifest that a great trade must be carried on by that system of railways to Sorel if, instead of finding entrance to Montreal over the Victoria bridge, it can find a harbour at Sorel. This will be the case not only with the trade in agricultural products, which is large, but with the trade of several thriving towns on those lines of railway, such as St. Johns, St. Hyacinthe and Iberville. But above all things it is an agricultural country, productive of all cereals except wheat, as well as butter, cheese and hay. I do not believe there is a more thriving population anywhere in Canada than in the valley of the Richelieu river. It is also connected with the Canada Atlantic, the Intercolonial and the South Shore Railways. Then, besides the counties I have mentioned, all the border counties of the St. Lawrence-Ya-maska, Nicolet, Lotbiniere-will be connected by railway with this harbour. When it has the facilities which it will have when this work is completed, it must have as a natural consequence a very large trade. We know from experience that when there are good natural conditions, and the accommodation is provided which is required by the modern means of traffic, the traffic will come. The province of Quebec up to the present time has had only two harbours-the harbour of Montreal and the harbour of Quebec. These harbours are going forward by leaps and bounds, but they are not the only harbours which are showing signs of progress. The harbour of Three Rivers will be one of the most important of the Dominion in a few years, and Sorel will be another. 19650,ca.proc.d.1901-05-09.4.6.223,1901-05-09,e94b8af3-fe69-477e-8184-ee47b287bc67,ca.m.6691,Mr. BENNETT.,,SUPPLY-ROYAL MINT.,WARREN Y. SOPER.,,Hon. gentlemen opposite will be delighted with the statement of the Minister of Public Works and the country will be astounded by it. His statement is this, that from this out it will be the policy of the department to erect and maintain public docks. I am aware that the hon. gentleman's department, since he has been in office, has been carrying out that policy. Let me mention some of the instances. Take one in the riding I represent. At a point called Hawkestone, a village of about 300 people, with a railway passing right through it, between Barrie and Orillia, and with no business there for a dock, the Postmaster General thought it advisable, in political interests, to erect a dock there costing about $2,500. What was the result? When that dock was about to be begun last fall, during the elections, I went to the village and told the people that it was a waste of money, and I instanced it as only one of the samples of bribery conducted wholesale by this government for the purpose of purchasing ridings. So strong was the feeling in that very district against the construction of the dock, that I got a majority there, where I had not a majority before. The people openly repudiated such barefaced expenditure of public money. I am not going to blame the Minister of Public Works for this, because he was simply an instrument in the hands of the Postmaster General. It was a disgrace to spend that money there, and Liberals right in that, district condemned the expenditure. They asked themselves if there was such barefaced waste of money there, what must there be all over the Dominion ?

A moment ago the hon. minister announced that he was spending $139,000 at Depot Harbour. Well, what are they doing at Depot Harbour to-day ? At that point Mr. Booth and the railway with which he is connected have a very large dock, on which they have erected a large elevator. What right has the Department of Public Works, 151

in the name of common sense, to take the money of the people and build a dock for Mr. Booth, which is to cost $139,000 ? What justification is there for permitting Mr. Booth, through the instrumentality of this government, to put his hand into the exchequer of the people and take out $139,000 for the construction of a dock which he wants, but does not want to construct himself ?

The hon. gentleman's department has been doing that kind of thing all along the north shore of Georgian Bay. At the village of Bruce Mines, a private party had a dock. A line of steamers called at that village, and no doubt, acting on business principles, went to the party who owned that dock and asked what rental the owner would charge to allow their boats to stop there. But the government, for political purposes, and no doubt in accord with the wishes of the hon. member who represents that county, spent at Bruce Mines $13,550 on the construction of a public dock. For what? Simply to let a line of boats call at it and make the dock of a private party utterly worthless. The hon. minister might as well go through the country and erect livery stables in every town and then hand them over to political friends and ruin the business of private parties.

In the Algoma district, the hon. minister spent upwards of $10,000 in the construction of a dock at the village of Hilton. There was a dock owned by a private party at Hilton, a political follower of the hon. gentleman. That dock had been purchased by him from a bankrupt estate for a mere song, and he unloaded it on this government for $5,000, and the hon. minister has since expended on that dock the large sum of $10,460 in addition to the $5,000.

When is this thing going to stop? The hon. member for West York (Mr. Wallace) took the Minister of Public Works at his word and asked where in the city of Toronto was there a government dock ? I challenge the hon. minister to name a single public dock in Toronto. What has been the case in Toronto ? Different parties have purchased the water lots on its water frontage, on which they have constructed docks, and when steamboat owners want to use these docks they make terms for the renting of them. That is a business proposition. But the Minister of Public Works says: We have hundreds of these docks. I know of only one dock constructed, in the section of country from which I come, by the late government, the dock at Beaverton. There was some little defence for that, because it was the only point which boats could seek as a refuge in a storm. Yet this work was condemned by hon. gentlemen opposite most vigorously as being a baiting and bribing of that constituency. Now the Minister of Public Works comes down and tells us that he is going to con-

struct docks wherever he pleases. They will be constructed either to meet political exigencies, as in the case of Mr. Booth, or to meet a large corporation which may happen to have influence with this government.

I see in the report of the Minister of Public Works that a dock has been constructed at a place called Keene in the riding of East Peterborough. When the vote for that work was before the House, I called the hon. minister's attention to it. What was his defence? Why, he did not know exactly where it was going to be constructed, and when I told him that it was to be erected on a creek, hardly the width of this room, what was the defence put forward by the hon. member for East Peterborough ? Was it that the work was necessary ? Not at all. His only defence was that they never had any money spent in that riding for docks, and he thought it about time there should be some. That was really the only reason why this expenditure was made at Keene, I think amounting to $2,500. The member for the riding admitted that there was no public necessity for it, but that it was simply being constructed because no public money had been expended there before.

So you can go all along this line of docks erected on the north shore of Georgian Bay. One and all of them were constructed to meet political exigencies just as that dock was constructed at Hawkestone.

What did the hon. gentleman do in the riding of North Simcoe? The hon. member for that riding made it one of his boasts in the last campaign that he was going to have a dock built in the town of Barrie where they had one already. But it was going to cause the expenditure of public money, and he thought that was ample justification.

Now the hon. gentleman is going to erect this large dock for Mr. Booth at Depot Harbour, where there is no public necessity for it, and where it will meet only the private needs of that gentleman. And the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Tarte) has laid down here to-night the dangerous and pernicious doctrine that, whenever he thinks lit, even though he may be moved by considerations of party exigencies, he will construct docks. The construction of harbour works is one thing, but the construction of docks for boats to call at is an entirely different thing. Where private parties have constructed docks and the receding of the waters has 'made it impossible to carry on traffic as before, it is quite right for the government to dredge in order that navigation may be carried on. But 1 dissent from the doctrine that the hon. gentleman should be allowed to go into any harbour in this country and build wharfs even though it may ruin private parties who already have docks built there. SOPER.,,That is a question that can be very easily settled by a reference to the expenditure of public money. If I am mistaken I am willing to make an apology. But, this is not the first time I have said that in thiis House. I have referred to it before when I was not so sharply corrected as I am to-night by the Minister of Public Works. I believed then, and I believe now, that on the lower St. Lawrence there are more docks constructed at the public, expense than there are in the province of Ontario. If I am wrong in that statement, I am willing to take it back when proof is offered. But, what I rose to say was, that not long ago the member for Frontenac, finding that condition of things, said while here : If there are going to be docks built at the public expense, I want one in my county. He applied to the government of the day to build a dock at the little village of Portsmouth, near Kingston, and a dock was built there by the late government, showing that the system was not initiated by the present government, but by tne preceding government. If I recollect aright, I said on a former occasion that the system was fraught with evil, not only on account of the original expenditure of public money for private purposes, but because the moment it was expended the government were bound to maintain the dock. I find now that what 1 said there has been borne out by what has taken place. The dock was built there by the late government, not so much, I think, in the interest of the great transportation question, but because the hon. gentleman who represented that county had the ear of the government. Last year, in order to prevent that dock from being positively dangerous, and entailing on the government, if not a legal liability, at all events a moral liability, for loss of life and limb, the present government had to spend a couple of thousand dollars in repairing and maintaining that dock. That is the state of things, and I close by saying what I wanted to say at the beginning, although hon. gentlemen seem to think that I have not made myself understood by the hon. minister. I do not understand, and I should be sorry to understand that this government intends to build a dock wherever it is not necessary. I can point to places all over the lake from Hamilton to the border line of Ontario, where docks have been built by individuals, and there has not been a dollar spent on any of these docks by the government. It will be unfair

to these men if a dock were to be built at the public expense in competition with them, and it would be unfair to the people of this Dominion were these private docks to be expropriated and put down as a charge upon the country. I do not understand that this is the intention of the government. So far as I gathered the hon. minister's meaning it is that wherever it is necessary for the development of the resources of the country and for the purpose of improving the navigation of the transportation routes to dredge a harbour, or perhaps to construct a dock, it is proposed, to that extent and to that extent only, to expend the money of the country and we cannot object to it.

I am informed there has been no appearance of difficulty since that time. I have stated clearly that Mr. Preston came here to attend to extremely important business in connection with immigration. It is a most important phase of the immigration question and most complicated, and nobody knew anything about it at the time Mr. Preston took up his work, because we were not able to get the information from our officers, and Lord Strathcona himself told me that it was quite impossible for him to give such atten-

tion to the details as would enable him to get the information. Mr. Preston has made himself master of all the facts in connection with it, which were most difficult to acquire, and he was here for the purpose of adjusting that question with the help of the department. He did not come here to do any political work or to waste his time. He came (here to do the business he is paid to do. When he was here he was subpoenaed by the Senate committee, and my deputy tells me that when the investigation was concluded Mr. Preston arranged to go westward, as he had been instructed to do before, for the purpose of getting further information respecting the foreign colonies in the Northwest. SOPER.,,The High Commissioner is not in my department or connected with it, except as being the head, officially or formally, of the immigration service. His office is, I believe, connected with the Department of the Secretary of State. His duties are of a general diplomatic character ; he represents Canada in all matters where an official representative is required. If my hon. friend will look at the debate which took place at the time when Sir Charles Tupper was appointed to the office of High Commissioner, he would get a full and clear exposition from the leadens of the House on the Conservative side of the duties the High Commissioner is expected to perform and the extreme necessity there was for the office at that time. I believe that the Prime Minister, the Finance Minister and other members of the government occasionally require to make use of the services of the High Commissioner, and they find him an officer of the greatest value to the Dominion, 'fhe office is especially valuable to the Dominion because we have occupying at the present time a gentleman of such strong personality and influence as Lord Strathcona, whose personal position in Great Britain lends great weight to the office. I do not suppose that my hon. friend desires to enter into details ais to the High Commissioner's duties, but outside of those to which I have referred, in a general way, he has superintendence of the office where Canadians go to register and where they

receive such information as they desire, and also where information iis asked by those who are interested in commercial questions connected with Canada. Particularly in relation to information to intending immigrants, Mr. Preston is supposed to have charge in the High Commissioner's office, and Mr. Colmer devotes his time to other work in connection with that office. The High Commissioner, I believe, shows in his report the correspondence of an official nature that takes place, and also the correspondence handled at the office for Canadians who are in Great Britain and in Europe. That is one of the duties that employs a great deal of the time of the clerks.

SOPER.,,The question of the location of the High Comissioner's office in London is one in which there is plenty of room for difference of opinion. The whole subject of the organization of our office in London is one that, in my judgment, will repay early attention. But, up to the present, it has not been decided by the government to make any permanent change. The office is in Victoria street, and is in what might be called the diplomatic portion of the city, and in the quarter where the colonies generally have their agencies. In this connection, the office is in the best place in the city. As an office for the receipt of questions respecting 152

matters of trade, it is not in the place where I would consider it to be best located. So far as immigration is concerned, it is not clear that a change would be of special benefit, though I understood from Mr. Preston, when I was there, that he was rather favourable to a change. My own opinion is, that the question of location is not an important one from the standpoint of immigration. As to its relation to matters of trade, as I have said, the question will repay consideration. My hon. friend is aware that it has been to some extent discussed in the press of this country, and that some of our people who have visited London on commercial affairs have been of opinion that a change ought to be made. I am not in a position to say whether such a change will be made, but it is a question upon which there is room for differences of opinion. The question of the location of the High Commissioner's office is one to which the High Commissioner himself has given some consideration lately, and I understood that there had been some communication, either to the Prime Minister or to the Secretary of State, on that subject. I do not know the result of that communication, but I am safe in saying that no removal from the present premises has been authorized.

SOPER.,,The remarks which Mr. Preston makes in this report to which my hon. friend refers, simply indicate that in his opinion there should be a rearrangement of the rooms in the building so that a portion might be exclusively devoted to immigration and commercial work, and if possible an exhibit should be displayed of the natural resources and products of this country. In the office of the High Commissioner at the present time there is no room for anything in the nature of an exhibit. But we have an exhibit at the present time In London, it is placed in the building known as the Imperial Institute. I have urged upon my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture to take official charge of that exhibit, and to make the necessary arrangements for re-

newing it and keeping it in the best order. The Imperial Institute contains exhibits from the various British colonies, and the arrangement with Canada was that the various provinces should place their exhibits and maintain them there directly, and this course has been followed heretofore. But I have urged, as a result of personal examination of the matter, that the Minister of Agriculture should take charge of it directly, because the various provinces have not given that attention to the matter which is desirable in order to keep the exhibits in proper shape. The exhibit in the Imperial Institute enables us in the city of London to direct people to a place where they can get a fair idea of the resources of Canada. With the exception of the fact that the Imperial Institute is not just where the High Commissioner's office is, I do not see what better arrangement could be made.

I have been trying to make the hon. member understand for the last twenty minutes that in an office of that kind you cannot put an exhibit that will give an adequate idea of the resources of the Dominion of Canada. Why, even in the industrial fair of Toronto you do not get an adequate idea of the industrial resources of Canada, you can only do that by travelling around. Minister of the Interior as to the duties of the High Commissioner, he was asked by the hon. member for East Elgin (Mr. Ingram) to state the duties of that officer and he did state a

number of things in a general way, but he said to the hon. member for East Elgin : If you want any particulars about the duties of the High Commissioner look at the date of the appointment of Sir Charles Tup-per and at the debate which occurred in parliament in reference thereto and you will find it very clearly set out, if you read the Conservative speeches, what the duties of the High Commissioner are. I would add that if you look at the speeches made on the opposite side, I have no doubt that what you would find would be how utterly worthless and useless this office was. As to the location of the office in London and as to the performance of duties in connection with immigration there, Mr. Willison, the editor of the Toronto Globe, who was over there a year or two ago, wrote very elaborately as to this particular question and his conclusion was that the location of the office was not what it should be for the purpose of promoting business and for promoting immigration. Furthermore, he held that the constitution of the office was not such as to promote either business or immigration to this country. I have been over there several times and have found it quite convenient for a Canadian visiting London in many ways to go there, but I cordially endorse what was said by Mr. Willison in the Globe, which he has elaborated with very great care and exactitude, that the arrangements for the promotion of business are not satisfactory at all. In the first place the location of the office is not suitable for business, and in the next place the machinery of the office it not adapted to the promotion of the commercial business which is required or to the business of immigration. The hon. minister simply sits and folds his arms. Some people may think this and some people may think that and he may think something else, but he has no positive opinion about it and he does not know. The minister ought to come here knowing something, he should have some positive opinions on the matter himself connected with the duties of this office. He ought to know, because he has been there himself, and he spent a great deal of his time there, I presume, whether the duties required in Great Britain on behalf of the Dominion of Canada are effectually and properly carried out under the present arrangements. We all know the distinguished position of the High Commissioner, Lord Strathcona. We all know his great patriotism, his love for Canada, and his efforts to make Canada appear well before the world. Those high qualities we know him to possess and we honour him for it, but we want the business of Canada carried on in other matters. The High Commissioner does not undertake to give that attention to commercial business and to immigration matters which the interests of Canada demand. These are the points that we are making and the hon. minister who has immigration matters under his control Mr. WALLACE.

simply has no opinion to give. He does not know whether it is this way or that way, though he has been over there and has made a personal inspection of these matters. He told us that he presumed Mr. Preston was sent for. He consulted his officers and he . said :
column2: Yes, Mr. Preston was sent for because we had some matters of the most important character that Mr. Preston alone could discuss with us. 19951,ca.proc.d.1901-05-09.4.7.43,1901-05-09,intervention,,,,SUPPLY-ROYAL MINT.,HAT 9, 1901 4837",,"So far as Ireland and Scotland are concerned, I can hold out no inducement that there will be any immediate reduction in the expenditure. I am perfectly satisfied that we would not get anybody at all from these countries if we did not maintain the staff in its present strength. When I visited the office last year, I made careful inquiry, and came to the conclusion that while we are not getting a large number, yet the people we were getting were obtained almost directly as the result of the work done, and they were people of an exceedingly good class. That information is corroborated by the hon. member for Selkirk, who was immigration commissioner at Winnipeg, and through whose hands most of these people passed. I do not regard the expenditure in Scotland as being excessive in view of the results. In 1900. we got 1.411 people. The railway companies in the United States reckon that on an average every settler they are able to get placed upon land in the vicinity of their railway lines costs about $500. We would think that we were incurring an enormous expenditure if we had to expend the one-half that amount. As the result of our work, we have succeeded in getting an immigration during the last year of 44,500 for an expenditure of $445, 000. or about $10 per head. And that includes the foreign expenditure, the expenditure in Canada taking care of the immigrants, the expenditure of the office at Winnipeg, the land guide, and all the officers charged with duties in that connection. So that the whole 44,500 people whom we secured as permanent settlers last year cost this country about $445,000. As I said, that includes every payment, bonuses to steamship companies and all others. Now, men who have given study to the subject of immigration will not agree with the view expressed by my hon. friend that you are to cease expenditure upon a particular place when you look at your returns and find that you are not getting many people from that place. If you are going to carry on an immigration work successfully, you will have to work the harder and spend the more money upon a locality when you get few people or none. You must keep at the work when the movement is low as well as when it is high. The movements that take place in different countries and at different times, and which ii: is impossible to control, will not yield you any advantage if you abandon the work as the non. gentleman suggests. In one year people move in large numbers from England, in another year they move in large numbers from Germany, and so on with other countries. If we are to carry on an immigration work at all- and I submit, as I said, that there is no

more important work undertaken by this government-we must spend our money and work away even when, in some years, we do not find that we realize what we might desire. If my hon. friend says that the immigration work of this government lias not been a success, I am bound to say that I do not agree with him in the least possible degree. When I took charge of the work of immigration in the fall of 189(1, I was told by the officers charged with the work that the immigration work was practically at a standstill, and I was told, to all intents and purposes, that it must remain at a standstill, that they could not suggest any way in which it could be successfully carried on. I want my hon. friend to look at the returns and he will find that from that day to this the immigration has steadily grown, and that we have now arrived at the point where we have forty or fifty thousand permanent settlers going upon our vacant lands every year. I am safe in saying that for the last three years that is about the number that have settled in Canada, and these are all, practically, settled in the North-west. Though we have had some people of the classes to which the hon. gentlemen on the other side have seen fit to take very strong objections-objections which, I think, have been well and fully and convincingly answered by my hon. friend from Selkirk (Mr. McCreary)-it is an entire mistake to suggest, as has been constantly done, that the Galicians and Doukhobors that have come to this country constitute the great bulk of the immigration we have received. They are a comparatively small proportion of that immigration. In the calendar year 1900, the immigration was as follows :

500. Now, hon. gentlemen opposite when in office undertook to work up immigration from the United States. The most utter and ridiculous failure that any government ever made in connection witti the operation of a department was made by the late government in its immigration operations in the United States. When I told the officers of the department that I purposed engaging in work in the United States, I was met with the smile which indicated that my predecessor had not been remarkably successful in that direction. I organized a staff of officers in the United States; and in tl'.e last calendar year we have received no less than 15,500 settlers from the United States, who settled upon the vacant lauds of the North-west and wrho are the very best class of settlers that can be got to fill up those lauds. I can tell the hon. gentleman that if he were on the line of the Calgary and Edmonton Railway, he would find people camped along that line, in some towns and villages occupying tents because they cannot find accommodation anywhere else. This influx of people is the direct result of the work we have been carrying on. It is an expensive work, I admit, but it cannot Mr. SIFTON.

be carried on in any other way. I do not believe that the people of Canada appreciate the value of the settlers who have been placed on the lands of the North-west Territories in the last four years. These settlers are producing in large quantities and will produce in much larger quantities; and are becoming some of the most reliable and valuable customers the people of eastern Canada have. My hon. friend from Lennox (Mr. Wilson) made a violent attack upon the government in connection with the Doukhobors and Galicians. A little afterwards, my attention was called to one fact which 1 will submit as an illustration of the results of placing settlers upon the vacant lands of the North-west Territories. In one settlement of Galician people-not United States settlers, who are very much in advance of the Galicians according to our ideas-the people purchased and paid for $150,000 worth of agricultural implements. Where were those implements made ? Almost exclusively in the province of Ontario. And those that were not made in that province were made in the United States and paid a substantial duty to the revenue of this country. I want my hon. friend to understand that though I do not take up much of the time of tills committee in the discussion of this subject, it is not because I feel that there is any apology needed for the work of the department or for its expenditure for the last five years. If he is disposed to go, we can start at the Red river and go through to the Rocky Mountains, and I can show him towns and villages that have been built up as a result of the work of the department. Yes, I will give him information of much more value than that which , he takes out of the Auditor General's Report, muddling his mind with the blue-books, as he is in the habit of doing. I can take him to places where, four years ago, there was nothing but bare prairie, and I can show him now thriving towns and villages. I can take him to one place which was almost uninhabited, and where, the last time I was there, I was told that within 30 miles there were no less than 8,000 actual farmers. I can take him to various places in the North-west Territories where, instead of the bare prairie, unproductive as it was, unproductive as it remained under the policy of hon. gentlemen, we have at the present time thriving and prosperous settlements. We have settlements where people are producing in large quantities agricultural produce. Now it is for the purpose of filling up that great domain that we are asking parliament to expend this money. You may be able, so long as there is a department of immigration, to go to the Auditor General's Report and to say that although in a particular year a good deal of money has been spent, yet very few people have been obtained. You might just as well expect that

a general could account for every bullet that was fired off In a battle as to expect the minister In charge of the immigration department to show settlers for every dollar that was expended. The work must be carried on under a general system of spreading information, and you have then to take your chances of a favourable result. An attempt to carry it on in any other way would result, as it did under the former government, after a lapse of years, in a dismal failure.

Now our hon. friends opposite find fault with a great many things, but they do not find fault apparently with the general results of our work, and they are not able to controvert the statement that in the course of the last four years the department has been successful in initiating a movement of people to Manitoba and the North-west Territories which is rapidly settling up that great country, and rapidly assuring the future of the Dominion of Canada. Sir, we all understand, and it has been admitted by those who have observed the national affairs of Canada with any degitee of attention, that the producing population of this country must be increased if the financial burdens of this country are to be easily borne, and it is by actual settlement of those prairie lands by an agricultural population that the burdens of Canada can be easily borne. We have been carrying on that work successfully, how successfully I have indicated by showing the numbers of people that we have received: and the indications are at the present time that from among the farmers of the western portion of the United States, there is an increasing movement, and we are likely to receive next year a much larger influx from that district than in the years past. Hon. gentlemen opposite will learn by inquiring from any gentleman who represents a North-west constituency that the people we have received from the western states are the very best settlers that any country can get. They are adapted for the work of prairie farmers, they have been trained in that direction, they are selfreliant. energetic, and in every respect they are calculated to be model citizens. We cannot have too many of them, and we are glad to know that the vacant lands of the Edmonton district, particularly, are being rapidly settled up by these people.

19955,ca.proc.d.1901-05-09.4.7.47,1901-05-09,7b93f979-f291-49f1-9a5c-54d08800f177,ca.m.2348,Mr. SPROULE.,,SUPPLY-ROYAL MINT.,HAT 9, 1901 4837",,"If the hon. gentleman was as well informed as he ought to be for a minister of the Crown, he would not make that statement, because if he knew the records of what took place before that time, he would know that Mr. Webster came year after year before the committee and showed photographs of train-load after train-load leaving the United States, bringing settlers and settlers' effects to Manitoba and the North-west Territories to settle there : and he in years afterwards read letter after letter showing their success in that country; yet the hon. gentleman stands up and says the policy was a failure. There were train-loads, some thireteen or seventeen cars, some with over twenty-three cars, and, if I remember correctly, there was one trainload of over thirty cars of settlers and their effects leaving at one time for Canada. That system was carried on successfully, and still the minister has the effrontery to say it was a dismal failure. He either knows or he does not know. If he knows, he made a statement which is disgraceful ; if he does not know, it is equally shameful for him to make a statement without knowledge, because it is an easy matter for him to ascertain the facts. Why was the immigration policy a failure to a large extent under the former government ? Because the expenditure for immigration was attacked year after year by the then opposition. I remember distinctly that under the attacks of the opposition during the Conser-

vatives' regime the appropriation for immigration was reduced year after year until it got down to $120,000. Could immigration be carried on successfully with that expenditure ? If the work has been going on and developing since, it is because this government is employing an army of agents. There are over 250 agents in the United States who are receiving pay for every man, woman and child they bring in. To-day this government is expending, not $120,000, but $445,000 for doing the same work for which they said a few years ago $120,000 was too much. The minister says the system was a failure, but they are carrying it on exactly on the same lines as their predecessors. We complain for one thing of the character of some of the agents they employ. We complained about the appointment of Mr. Jury in England. JWe said it was unwise to take a tailor from Canada and make an immigration agent of him in England, and our complaint was justified. Now, we are not condemning the principle of immigration, we do not say that money should not he expended for that purpose; but we are condemning the system upon which the work is now carried on in some lines.

,Conservative (1867-1942),,Thomas Simpson Sproule,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=7b93f979-f291-49f1-9a5c-54d08800f177&Language=E&Section=ALL

I have to tell my hon. friend that I differ from him. I do know. 19958,ca.proc.d.1901-05-09.4.7.50,1901-05-09,intervention,,,,SUPPLY-ROYAL MINT.,HAT 9, 1901 4837",,"I am speaking of that which I know and of that which the hon. gentleman knows absolutely nothing. The hon. gentleman says that we have in the United States at the present time something like 200 immigration agents. He leaves the impression on the minds of the members of the committee that we are paying salaries to 200 agents. He did not say that, but that is the impression that he sought to impart. The number of salaried agents that we have in the United States is. I think, 22 and the large number Mr. SPROULE.

of agents to which the hon. gentleman refers are not salaried agents at all but agents who are paid for the actual number of people they send in here and settle in the country. I fancy every member of the committee will admit that it is a businesslike proceeding to employ these people in this way, so that we shall not pay them for what we do not get. I want to say one word on a question which has been before the committee in respect to matters affecting immigration a good many times in the four years that I have had charge of that branch. I have had occasion to appoint a number of gentlemen to this service who have rendered political services to the Liberal party and in consequence of the fact that I have appointed to this branch of the public service, certain gentlemen who have rendered political services to the Liberal party, I have been very bitterly assailed by hon. gentlemen opposite and these hon. gentlemen, upon every occasion that the immigration estimates are before the House, seek, as my hon. friend says, to attack certain phases of that immigration work, and the phase of that immigration work which my hon. friends seeks to attack consists in the appointment to office of gentlemen who have been unfortunate enough, from his standpoint, to render political services to the Liberal party. I will say this to my hon. friend in all confidence, that I am afraid my hon. friend and myself will never be able to agree upon that question. I am afraid that so long as I have charge of that branch of the service and there are officers required and there are capable and intelligent men upon the Liberal side, who have rendered services to the Liberal party, I shall be compelled to offend the sensibilities of the hon. gentleman and appoint these men to office. I want to say to my hon. friend that I do not regard the fact that a man has occupied a somewhat prominent position in the organization of the Liberal party and has been regarded as a capable, intelligent, experienced, and valuable man by the Liberal party, that that is any reason why he should not be appointed to the public service. But, other things being equal, I regard a man of that kind as likely to be a good public servant. I believe that the same capability and intelligence which make him a valuable man in connection with political affairs make him a valuable public servant Let me say to my hon. friends that if they had done as I have done, if when they appointed their immigration agents in the United States, instead of picking out the political friends who were of no use to them, who had never been any use to them and putting them at this work, they had picked out some of the men who had shown themselves to be good men, their work would have been more successful and successful probably to the same extent that ours has been. I can assure my hon. friend that we have only taken men of the very best class in connection with our immigra-

tion work, and if lion, gentlemen keep on attacking these gentlemen we shall be forced to the conclusion that it is the recollection of the exceedingly valuable work which these gentlemen did when they were actively engaged in politics that makes hon. gentlemen opposite so determined to attack them now. I do not know that there is anything more to be said on this phase of the question, but I feel bound to reiterate the statement that I am afraid that I am not a very likely subject of conversion to the view to which the hon. gentleman referred, and I am afraid that he will not be able to succeed in inducing me to cease the practice which hon. gentlemen, no doubt, regard as very reprehensible, of appointing Liberals to office when there are vacancies to be filled.

There are one or two letters that I have received, dealing with the same subject. I have a letter from Messrs. La Rue & Picard, of Edmonton, a firm amongst the most extensive dealers in that town, who do business with the Galicians. They say :

Regarding information as to the new colony of Galicians and Russian peoples, we are glad to state that they are reliable in all points of view, intelligent, hardworking and honest. Having had occasion many times to deal with them, we have always found that they were improving all the time, so we can recojpmend them as one of the best immigration peoples of our country.
Yours truly,
(S3.) LaRUE & PICARD.

Next to the Hudson's Bay Company and to McDougall & Secord, they are the largest merchants in Edmonton. I think this evidence is sufficient to convince the committee that the statements that I made about these people were absolutely correct. 1 would just say a word in regard to the Doukhobors. There was something said to the effect that these people were not desirable immigrants, and in that connection I would like to read a resolution that was passed by the Board of Trade of Yorkton, at the time these people were about to be removed from Yorkton. This resolution is dated April 3rd, 1900, and it reads as follows :

Whereas, it has come to our knowledge that a representative of the Northern Pacific Railway is at present in this district for the purpose of encouraging the Doukhobors to move to California, it is moved by William Simpson, seconded by J. J. Smith, that we strongly protest against such proceedings on the part of any railroad company which has in the past and may in the future receive government aid, and (bat a copy of this resolution be sent to the Northern Pacific Railway, Winnipeg, the
Commissioner of Immigration, and the Winnipeg daily papers.
(Sgd.) W. D. DUNLOP,

Hon. gentlemen talk about immigration as it is carried on by this government, but I noticed the other day a very peculiar circumstance that occurred in connection with the Manitoba government. The gentleman who ran against me in the recent election, Mr. Haslam, was not a thorough-going Conservative according to Mr. Roblin's idea, and a little row has taken place between him and Mr. Roblin. Mr. Roblin said that he was a disgruntled politician, that because he wais not appointed an immigration agent lie turned against his party.
